title: Microsoft Fabric vs Azure Synapse: Full Comparison & Limitations
summary: An independent comparison blog positioning Microsoft Fabric as the SaaS successor to Azure Synapse Analytics' PaaS model, itemizing feature gaps (notably around Spark and dedicated SQL pools) and outlining migration paths between the two platforms.
audience: Architects and platform teams currently on Azure Synapse Analytics deciding whether and how to move workloads to Microsoft Fabric.
why_it_matters: This is a rare comparison post that explicitly enumerates concrete Fabric gaps versus Synapse (rather than only selling Fabric's strengths), which is useful for a balanced migration risk assessment, though its specific dates and figures are unverified and were excluded here.
takeaways: Fabric is positioned by the post (citing a Microsoft executive statement) as the successor to Synapse rather than a separate competing product, with Synapse remaining supported but not the recommended starting point for new work.
The most cited hard gap is Fabric Spark's lack of .NET-for-Spark (C#/F#) support, which the post calls a blocker requiring a rewrite to Python or Scala before migration.
Fabric's Data Warehouse is serverless-only; there is no dedicated-SQL-pool equivalent, so workloads relying on DWU-based fixed capacity need a different sizing approach.
A public-preview Pipeline Migration Assistant is described as doing an assessment-first, non-destructive conversion of Synapse pipelines into Fabric Data Factory artifacts.
Synapse Link's replacement in Fabric is mirroring, but the post flags this as having some source-coverage gaps relative to Synapse Link at the time of writing.

claims.text: The post frames Fabric as a SaaS platform with a single control plane and unified OneLake storage, contrasted with Synapse's PaaS model of modular components (dedicated SQL pools, separate Spark pools) with more granular but separately managed configuration.

Fabric Spark does not support .NET for Spark (C# or F#), which the post identifies as a hard blocker for teams with existing .NET Spark workloads migrating from Synapse, requiring a rewrite to Python or Scala.

Fabric's Data Warehouse is described as serverless-only with automatic scaling and no dedicated, isolated resource-pool option, unlike Synapse's DWU-based dedicated SQL pools which offer predictable, isolated capacity.
The post notes Fabric Data Warehouse background operations use a 24-hour compute-smoothing window, which is a different consumption model than Synapse's fixed DWU allocation.

A Pipeline Migration Assistant (in public preview per the post) performs an assessment-first migration of Synapse pipelines into Fabric Data Factory: it checks activity compatibility, converts linked services into Fabric connections, and disables migrated triggers by default so they can be validated before activation.

Synapse notebooks and Spark job definitions (.ipynb, .py, .R, .jar) are described as importable directly into Fabric, while UI-based JSON import/export of Spark job definitions available in Synapse is not available in Fabric, where Git-based workflows are used instead.

The post positions Fabric mirroring as the successor to Azure Synapse Link, covering sources such as Azure SQL, PostgreSQL, Cosmos DB, and Snowflake, but flags some coverage gaps relative to Synapse Link at the time of writing.

The post contrasts Fabric's native Eventstream-plus-Eventhouse real-time analytics stack (built on KQL) with Synapse's reliance on separate Event Hubs and Stream Analytics services, describing Fabric's integration as tighter by default.

Migrating from Synapse dedicated SQL pools to Fabric Warehouse has no automated migration tool per the post; it describes using CETAS (Create External Table As Select) as a manual data-movement pattern.
